description: Alberta’s staged licensing program that allows new drivers to gain skills and experience under controlled conditions.
The first GDL stage, allowing supervised driving under learner conditions.
A probationary licence held during the second stage of Alberta’s GDL program.
A non-GDL licence permitting independent operation of cars and other eligible light vehicles.
A computerized multiple-choice test covering road rules, safe driving practices, and road signs.
A practical assessment of vehicle handling, observation, judgement, and compliance with road rules.
A required check confirming that a driver meets Alberta’s minimum vision standards.
An authorized Alberta office providing services such as licensing, registration, testing, and licence updates.
A person authorized to conduct road tests and assess whether applicants have the required driving skills.
A licence endorsement required to operate vehicles with air-only or combined air and hydraulic brakes.
A code placed on a licence to identify a special driving requirement, such as corrective lenses.
A code showing that a driver has completed specific training or may operate specially equipped vehicles.
Points recorded against a driving record following conviction for certain traffic offences.
An official record showing driving convictions, suspensions, and other licensing information.
A red, yellow, or green light used to control traffic flow at intersections or merging roadways.
A signal requiring a complete stop before the stop line, crosswalk, or intersection.
A warning that the signal is changing to red and drivers must stop unless stopping cannot be done safely.
A signal permitting movement through an intersection while still requiring applicable yielding.
A signal treated like a stop sign, requiring a complete stop followed by yielding before proceeding.
A signal allowing drivers to proceed cautiously after yielding to traffic and pedestrians.
A signal allowing movement or turns without stopping while requiring drivers to yield to lawful road users.
An overhead red X or green arrow controlling whether a lane is closed or available in the indicated direction.
A sign indicating what road users must or must not do, including speed, turn, parking, and access rules.
A sign providing advance notice of a hazard, road condition, intersection, crossing, or required action.
A white square with a green circle showing that the indicated action is permitted.
A white sign with a red circle and diagonal bar showing that the indicated action is prohibited.
A regulatory sign requiring a complete stop and yielding before proceeding safely.
A sign requiring a driver to slow, be prepared to stop, and give right-of-way where necessary.
The maximum legal speed under ideal conditions, not necessarily a safe speed in poor conditions.
An area marked with a school sign and posted speed limit where special speed and passing restrictions apply.
An area marked by a school sign without an attached speed sign, warning drivers to use caution.
An area with a playground sign and posted speed limit where reduced-speed and passing restrictions apply.
An area marked by a playground sign without a speed sign, warning that children may be nearby.
A roadway work area where posted speeds, warning signs, and flag-person directions must be obeyed.
A lane designated for specified road users, such as buses, taxis, bicycles, or high-occupancy vehicles.
A pavement marking that generally prohibits crossing to pass or change lanes.
A pavement marking that permits crossing to pass or change lanes when it is safe.
A pavement marking separating traffic travelling in opposite directions.
A pavement marking separating traffic travelling in the same direction.
A pavement marking showing where a vehicle must stop at an intersection or railway crossing.
A marked or unmarked area where pedestrians cross and drivers must yield as required.
A marked lane reserved for cyclists that motor vehicles may enter only where permitted, such as for turning.
A travel lane marked to remind drivers that cyclists may use the same lane.
An area beside or slightly behind a vehicle that cannot be seen in its mirrors.
A quick glance over the shoulder to check an area that cannot be seen in the mirrors.
Open space maintained around a vehicle to provide room for stopping or avoiding hazards.
The time and space maintained between your vehicle and the vehicle ahead.
The minimum recommended following time under normal road and weather conditions.
The time required to recognize a situation and understand that stopping or another response is needed.
The time required to respond to a hazard, such as moving a foot from the accelerator to the brake.
The distance a vehicle travels after its brakes are applied until it stops.
The combined distance travelled during perception, reaction, and braking.
Firm braking to the point just before the wheels lock, preserving the ability to steer.
A system that cycles brake pressure to help prevent wheel lock and preserve steering control.
The clutch position where a manual transmission begins connecting engine power to the wheels.
Unnecessarily resting a foot on the clutch pedal, causing additional clutch wear.
Parking parallel to the curb in a space between vehicles.
Parking in a stall positioned diagonally, commonly at approximately 45 degrees to the traffic lane.
Parking in a stall positioned at a 90-degree angle to the curb.
Rules determining which road user must yield and which may proceed.
An intersection regulated by traffic signs, traffic signals, or both.
An intersection without signs or signals where drivers generally yield to the vehicle on their right.
A three- or four-way stop where the first vehicle to arrive proceeds first, or the vehicle on the right proceeds when arrivals are simultaneous.
A circular intersection where traffic travels counterclockwise and entering vehicles yield to traffic already inside.
A circular intersection designed with tighter curves to encourage lower speeds.
A turn made from one of two marked turning lanes into its corresponding destination lane.
A shared centre lane used by traffic from either direction when preparing to turn left.
A manoeuvre that turns a vehicle around to travel in the opposite direction using oncoming lanes.
An additional highway lane allowing faster traffic to pass slower vehicles safely.
The highway shoulder reserved for urgent stops or vehicle problems, not normal driving or passing.
A lane used to increase speed and match the flow of traffic before merging onto a roadway.
A lane used to reduce speed when exiting a highway or major roadway.
The shared process of safely blending traffic where two roadways join into one.
A shared lane where entering traffic accelerates while exiting traffic slows.
A loss of vehicle control caused by reduced tire traction.
A skid caused when braking locks the wheels of a vehicle without ABS.
A skid caused by accelerating too quickly and making the drive wheels spin.
A sideways slide caused by travelling too quickly while turning.
Loss of tire contact with a wet road surface, which can cause loss of vehicle control.
A difficult-to-see layer of ice formed when moisture freezes on the road.
The controlled process of slowing and gradually returning to the roadway after leaving the pavement.
Four-way flashing lights used to warn others that a vehicle is stopped or presents a hazard.
Anticipating hazards and acting early to reduce, minimize, or avoid danger.
The distance measured in seconds that a driver scans ahead to allow time to respond to hazards.
A permanent roadway condition, such as a curve, hill, intersection, or hidden driveway.
A changing condition, such as pedestrians, icy surfaces, emergency vehicles, or stale green lights.
Driving while attention is diverted by activities such as phone use, texting, reading, programming devices, or grooming.
An approved restraint selected for a child’s age or weight and installed according to manufacturer instructions.
A universal anchor system used to secure compatible child safety seats to a vehicle.
An approved seat that positions a child correctly for use of the vehicle’s seat belt.
A pedestrian, cyclist, or motorcycle rider with less physical protection than an enclosed-vehicle occupant.
Alternating warning lights indicating that a school bus is slowing and preparing to stop.
Alternating lights requiring applicable traffic to stop while students enter, leave, or cross near the bus.
Flashing amber and red lights indicating that a snowplow is operating ahead.
A location where a road crosses railway tracks and drivers must yield to trains.
An X-shaped railway crossing sign requiring drivers to yield to trains.
A quiet electrically powered rail system whose crossings must be treated like other railway crossings.
A closely grouped line of vehicles with headlights on that may proceed together through an intersection when safe.
Operating a vehicle while alcohol, drugs, medication, or another condition reduces driving ability.
Alberta’s escalating administrative penalty program for impaired driving.
A zero-tolerance alcohol and drug program for Class 7 learner and Class 5-GDL drivers.
A zero-tolerance alcohol and drug program for commercial drivers operating in a commercial capacity.
Roadside sanctions applying when a driver’s blood alcohol concentration reaches the specified warning threshold.
Serious roadside sanctions applying to criminal-level impairment, prohibited concentrations, or refusal of a lawful demand.
A device measuring breath alcohol and preventing a vehicle from starting when the reading exceeds its threshold.
The administrative branch that reviews challenges to provincial impaired-driving penalties and vehicle seizures.
The process used to request reviews of non-impaired-driving administrative decisions.
Securely fastened chains crossed beneath a trailer tongue to provide a secondary connection.
A trailer safety system designed to activate if the trailer separates from the towing vehicle.
The tendency of trailer wheels to follow a path inside the path taken by the towing vehicle’s wheels.
